title: Market stall allocation
brief:
Write an allocation report for the manager of an indoor Saturday market. Fictional totals from eight Saturdays give stall bookings, stalls actually opened, anonymous shopper requests for more vendors, and average gross sales per opened stall. Produce: 72, 69, 43, $460. Bakery: 48, 46, 28, $390. Prepared food: 40, 34, 39, $520. Crafts: 56, 51, 16, $210. Each Saturday has 30 pitches, only six of which have power. Every prepared-food stall and half of booked bakery stalls need power, rounded up. Keep at least four pitches per category. Compare demand and reliability, propose and justify a pitch allocation, and explain how the manager should handle cancellations and evaluate the change.

Aim for 1,200 to 1,800 words. Return the complete original work directly in your answer. Do not sign or identify yourself. Do not use tools.

b9510acd392c0bd1.text:
# Saturday market pitch allocation report

For the next eight Saturdays, offer **14 pitches for produce, four for bakery, four for prepared food and eight for crafts**. Treat these numbers as opening offers for each date, then release unclaimed pitches to eligible vendors. Reserve four powered pitches for prepared food and two for bakery. The six power connections determine how many bakery and prepared-food stalls the market can book. The main decision the manager can test with the existing facilities is how to fill the other 22 pitches.

## What the eight Saturdays show

The market recorded 216 bookings and 200 openings across 240 available pitch-days. An average Saturday therefore had 27 bookings and 25 open stalls. Of the 40 pitch-days without an open stall, 24 had no booking and 16 had a booking that did not result in an opening. The manager has two distinct opportunities to improve the market. Earlier recruitment can fill pitches that attract no booking, while a standby system can recover pitches when a booked vendor cancels.

| Category | Bookings | Stalls opened | Openings per booking | Average openings per Saturday | Shopper requests | Average gross sales per opened stall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Produce | 72 | 69 | 95.8% | 8.63 | 43 | $460 |
| Bakery | 48 | 46 | 95.8% | 5.75 | 28 | $390 |
| Prepared food | 40 | 34 | 85.0% | 4.25 | 39 | $520 |
| Crafts | 56 | 51 | 91.1% | 6.38 | 16 | $210 |

Produce makes the strongest case for additional space. It drew the most bookings, opened on 69 of 72 occasions and still attracted the largest number of requests for more vendors. Its average gross sales were also second highest. Those signals reinforce each other. Shoppers asked for more produce even though they already saw more produce stalls than stalls of any other category. The uncertainty is on the vendor side. Fourteen offers would be five more than the historical average of nine produce bookings each week. Filling them will require recruitment.

Prepared food presents the sharpest trade-off. It generated 39 requests with only 34 openings, and its $520 average gross sales led the market. Yet six of its 40 bookings failed to produce an open stall, the largest shortfall in both number and percentage terms. A prepared-food cancellation can therefore leave shoppers with fewer choices in a category they frequently asked the market to expand. It also leaves a scarce powered pitch vacant unless the manager can find a suitable replacement in time.

Bakery matched produce for reliability and averaged six bookings per Saturday. Reducing its initial offer to four has a real cost for vendors and shoppers, particularly given the 28 requests for additional bakers. Crafts generated the fewest requests and the lowest average sales, but craft vendors supplied 51 openings, more than either bakery or prepared food. Their participation gives the manager a credible way to fill unpowered space. Anonymous requests measure expressed interest and may include repeat shoppers. Gross sales measure takings before costs. Neither measure establishes what an additional vendor would earn.

## How to allocate the pitches

| Category | Initial pitches per Saturday | Powered | Unpowered |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Produce | 14 | 0 | 14 |
| Bakery | 4 | 2 | 2 |
| Prepared food | 4 | 4 | 0 |
| Crafts | 8 | 0 | 8 |
| **Total** | **30** | **6** | **24** |

The four-pitch minimum for prepared food commits four power connections. Four bakery bookings require the remaining two. A fifth bakery booking would raise its requirement to three because half of five rounds up. A fifth prepared-food booking would require a fifth connection for that category alone. Either change would take the combined requirement to seven. Four bookings apiece are consequently both the minimum and the maximum for these categories while the manager preserves all four category floors. The two unpowered bakery places should go to vendors who confirm they can operate in them.

The historical booking totals reveal a discrepancy worth checking before issuing offers. Forty prepared-food bookings would have required 40 powered pitch-days. The 48 bakery bookings would have required at least another 24, potentially more after rounding on individual Saturdays. That makes at least 64 powered pitch-days against 48 available over eight weeks. If the figures count successive bookings for the same pitch after cancellations, some of the apparent overlap may disappear. The manager should check dated rosters and power assignments to establish what happened. The proposed allocation fits the stated limit on every Saturday without relying on expected absences.

Of the 22 produce and craft pitches, the proposed split gives crafts one more offer than its historical average of seven bookings and directs the other five offers above those categories’ combined historical average toward produce. This favors the category with stronger shopper interest while leaving room for modest craft growth. It also makes the choice reversible. If only ten produce vendors book for a particular date and craft vendors are waiting, keeping four usable pitches empty would do little for shoppers. Once the initial booking window closes, the manager should offer those pitches to the waiting vendors while continuing produce recruitment for later dates.

## Handling cancellations and vacancies

At booking, record the date, category, power requirement and a contact number for each vendor. Maintain a separate standby list for each Saturday so that an offer goes to someone who has already indicated availability for that date. For bakery, mark which standby vendors can trade without power. For prepared food, ask how much notice each vendor needs to prepare stock. A vendor who can accept on Thursday may be unable to deliver the same offer on Saturday morning.

Send a confirmation request early enough to act on the reply, for example on Wednesday, with a Thursday response deadline. Tell vendors the deadline and release procedure when they book. Follow up once on an unanswered confirmation, then release the pitch under the published terms. Give a standby vendor a stated time to accept before approaching the next person. Record when the manager learned of a vacancy and when a replacement accepted. Those times will show whether an earlier reminder is likely to recover more openings.

Replace cancellations within the same category first, matching the available power. A cancellation by an unpowered baker leaves an unpowered place. A prepared-food cancellation leaves a powered place that should go first to another prepared-food vendor. When a category is already at its four-pitch floor, keep the place designated for that category through the replacement process. If nobody eligible can attend, record the vacancy and the shortfall in actual openings. The manager can reserve four pitches and recruit standbys, but attendance ultimately depends on vendors. For produce and crafts above their floors, release an unfilled place across categories when the original list is exhausted. Avoid double-booking against an expected cancellation because all confirmed vendors could arrive.

## Evaluating the change

Run the allocation for eight Saturdays and review the roster after each market. The primary comparison is actual openings against the previous average of 25 per Saturday. Keep separate counts for pitches offered, confirmed bookings, cancellations, replacements and stalls that opened. A recovered cancellation should count as one open pitch even if two vendors held the booking at different times. Record weekly totals as well as the eight-week average so the manager can see whether an apparent improvement depended on one unusually busy Saturday.

Judge the produce expansion by how many of its 14 offers become openings, how often a produce place passes to crafts and what sellers earn as the category grows. Collect sales on the same basis as before and note how many open stalls report. Track both average sales per reporting stall and combined reported sales for the category. Together they can show whether extra vendors appear to bring additional trade or divide similar takings among more sellers. Repeat the shopper question in the same place and manner each week, recording the number of respondents so changes in request counts can be interpreted alongside changes in participation.

At the end of the trial, retain the 14-to-eight split if produce regularly fills its offers and shopper and sales figures support the expansion. If produce places repeatedly pass to waiting craft vendors, move an initial offer to crafts and review the resulting openings. For bakery and prepared food, count eligible vendors turned away for lack of power and Saturdays on which all six powered pitches actually operated. Repeated turnaways alongside full use and continuing shopper requests would give the manager a concrete basis for pricing additional electrical capacity. Frequent powered vacancies after late cancellations would instead make faster replacement the immediate priority.

c393a9a2b6469a90.text:
# Saturday market pitch allocation report

## Recommended allocation

For the next eight Saturdays, offer **13 produce pitches, four bakery pitches, four prepared-food pitches, and nine crafts pitches**. Assign four of the six powered pitches to prepared food and two to bakery. This uses all 30 pitches and preserves the four-pitch minimum in every category. Treat these figures as the initial offer each week. After the booking deadline, release surplus unpowered pitches above a category’s four-pitch minimum to vendors on the compatible waiting list.

Produce has the strongest case for expansion. It leads in bookings and shopper requests, and almost 96% of its bookings opened. Crafts has the second-highest booking volume and can use the remaining unpowered space, although shopper requests and average sales suggest opening those pitches to produce if crafts demand falls short. Bakery and prepared food both show demand beyond the proposed offer. Their allocation is governed by the supply of power.

## Demand and reliability

| Category | Bookings | Opened | Share of bookings that opened | Shopper requests for more vendors | Average gross sales per opened stall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Produce | 72 | 69 | 95.8% | 43 | $460 |
| Bakery | 48 | 46 | 95.8% | 28 | $390 |
| Prepared food | 40 | 34 | 85.0% | 39 | $520 |
| Crafts | 56 | 51 | 91.1% | 16 | $210 |
| **Total** | **216** | **200** | **92.6%** | **126** | |

The market averaged 27 bookings and 25 opened stalls per Saturday. The gap between bookings and openings averaged two stalls per week. The totals do not distinguish advance cancellations from late cancellations or no-shows. That distinction matters because a vendor who cancels early gives the manager a chance to refill the pitch.

Produce averaged nine bookings and 8.6 openings per Saturday. It received the most requests for more vendors and generated $460 per opened stall, second only to prepared food. Those signals support giving produce first claim on expansion space. Thirteen pitches provide room for four more bookings than its historical weekly average. The figures support offering that room, while the pilot will establish how often vendors take it up.

Bakery averaged six bookings and 5.75 openings per Saturday and tied produce for the highest opening rate. Four pitches will therefore put pressure on an otherwise dependable category. Prepared food averaged five bookings and 4.25 openings per Saturday. It received 39 shopper requests, only four fewer than produce, and had the highest average gross sales at $520 per opened stall. It also accounted for six of the 16 bookings that did not open, the largest count of any category. Keeping four prepared-food pitches serves clear shopper interest. A waiting list gives the manager a way to protect that offer when a vendor cancels.

Crafts averaged seven bookings and about 6.4 openings per Saturday. Its 56 bookings indicate a substantial pool of vendors, while its 16 shopper requests and $210 average gross sales give it a weaker case for expansion than produce. Offering nine pitches gives crafts room to absorb about two more weekly bookings than its historical average. The booking deadline gives the manager an opportunity to move unused space to a category with vendors ready to open.

The measures answer different questions. Bookings show how much space vendors secured under the earlier arrangement. Shopper requests show where respondents wanted more choice, and anonymous counts cannot establish how many distinct shoppers made those requests. Gross sales show how much vendors sold per opening. They do not establish profit, market income, or what an additional stall would sell.

## How power determines the allocation

Four prepared-food bookings require four powered pitches. Four bakery bookings require two, since half of four is two. A fifth bakery booking would raise the bakery requirement to three powered pitches after rounding up. A fifth prepared-food booking would also require a seventh powered pitch with four bakery bookings in place. With at least four pitches to offer in each category, the proposed split commits all six powered pitches on a fully booked Saturday.

The historical figures also need checking before they are used as a baseline for power use. Forty prepared-food bookings would have required 40 powered placements. The 48 bakery bookings would have required at least 24 more, since rounding each Saturday up can only increase the total. That is a minimum of 64 powered bookings across eight Saturdays, compared with 48 powered pitch-days available. The aggregate figures cannot show how that mismatch arose. The manager should check the old pitch records and confirm which power rules and facilities applied. For the pilot, the manager should calculate power requirements separately for each Saturday and record the pitch assigned to every vendor who needs power.

## Handling cancellations and empty pitches

Ask vendors to confirm by Thursday at noon and provide one clear way to cancel. At booking, tell vendors when the market will release an unconfirmed pitch and how quickly they need to answer a waiting-list offer. Record each vendor’s category, contact details, power requirement, and ability to accept a Friday or Saturday opening. Ask who can arrive with enough time to set up safely.

Offer a cancelled pitch first to a compatible vendor in the same category, in waiting-list order, and give the vendor a clear response deadline. For prepared food, the replacement needs a powered pitch. For bakery, check the replacement’s equipment and recalculate the rounded-up power requirement using the updated bakery booking count. Keep the pitch assignments and booking list together so that a replacement is confirmed only once the manager knows where the vendor can trade. Use one confirmed booking per pitch.

At the Thursday deadline, make any surplus unpowered pitch above a category’s four-pitch minimum available to the other unpowered category with a ready vendor. For example, if crafts confirms seven vendors and produce has two vendors waiting, move two unpowered pitches to produce for that Saturday. Keep the four-pitch minimum available to each category through the replacement process. If a late cancellation leaves one of those pitches empty, record the vacancy and the attempts to fill it. On Saturday morning, use the short-notice waiting list up to the setup cutoff. Record any remaining no-show separately from a cancellation received in time to offer the pitch again.

## Evaluating the change

Run the allocation for eight Saturdays and review the records after week four for practical problems with confirmation, replacement timing, or power assignments. For each category and Saturday, log the initial offer, booking requests, confirmed bookings, vendors turned away, openings, and vacancies. Distinguish vendors turned away for lack of power from those turned away for lack of ordinary space. Record when a vendor cancelled, whether the pitch was offered again, and whether the replacement opened. Count each pitch once in the opening figures, even if several vendors booked it in succession.

The main outcome is how many pitches actually open, compared with the historical average of 25 out of 30. Also compare openings by category and track how often the extra produce and crafts pitches are used. If the market fills more pitches while bakery and prepared-food waiting lists grow, report both results. A higher overall opening count can coexist with unmet demand for powered stalls. Track the share of cancelled pitches that replacements opened, along with the raw counts, so a few early cancellations do not obscure a persistent problem with late ones.

Repeat the shopper question in the same locations and at similar times, and record the number of responses so requests for each category can be compared as a share of respondents. Collect average gross sales per opened stall by category and track total reported gross sales alongside it. A category can bring in more sales overall while individual vendors sell less, which matters when deciding whether to keep its extra pitches. Note unusual events or disruptions that may explain a single Saturday’s results.

Keep the allocation if the extra pitches regularly open, overall openings improve, and the shopper and sales figures support the resulting mix. If crafts repeatedly leaves space empty while produce turns away vendors, adjust the starting split for the next period. If both categories leave space empty while bakery and prepared food maintain waiting lists, document how many bookings the six powered pitches prevented. That gives the manager a basis for deciding whether additional power capacity is worth investigating.
